Q117.L1t: Special relativity says that lengths and time intervals measured in one frame differ from those measured in a frame moving relative to it.
Q117.L2t: The length of an object along its direction of motion is measured to be shorter by the factor 1/γ, where γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²), compared with its rest length.
Q117.L3t: At 0.8c the Lorentz factor is 5/3, so the observer sees a stick 0.6 m long, and the passing time is this contracted length divided by the speed 0.8c.
Q117.L4t: The stick takes about 2.5 nanoseconds to pass the observer.
Q117.L2f: A moving object's length along its direction of motion is measured to be longer than its rest length by the factor γ.
Q117.L3f: The observer must apply the 0.6 contraction factor twice, once to shorten the stick and again to shorten the passing time, which gives a much smaller time.
Q117.L4f: The stick takes about 1.6 nanoseconds to pass the observer.

Q118.L1t: Capacitors store charge and energy, and combining them in series or parallel changes the effective capacitance of the circuit.
Q118.L2t: Once the first capacitor is disconnected from the battery, the total charge on the system is fixed and can only be redistributed.
Q118.L3t: Two identical capacitors in series act as half a capacitor, and when this pair is joined in parallel with the first, the original charge CV₀ is shared across a total capacitance of 3C/2 at one common voltage.
Q118.L4t: The final voltage on the first capacitor is two-thirds of its initial voltage.
Q118.L2f: When capacitors are connected in series their capacitances add directly, while in parallel the reciprocals add.
Q118.L3f: Two identical capacitors in series behave like a single capacitor of four times the original capacitance, so the original charge spreads over a total of five capacitor units.
Q118.L4f: The final voltage on the first capacitor is one-fifth of its initial voltage.

Q119.L1t: When fast electrons strike a metal target they lose energy in several ways, producing both a continuous X-ray spectrum and discrete spectral lines.
Q119.L2t: The continuous background of the X-ray spectrum comes from bremsstrahlung, which is radiation emitted as electrons are decelerated by the atoms of the target.
Q119.L3t: The sharp lines have energies fixed by the differences between atomic energy levels of the target metal, so they must come from transitions of electrons between atomic shells after an inner electron has been knocked out.
Q119.L4t: Characteristic X rays are emitted when electrons drop into vacancies left in the inner shells of the metal atoms.
Q119.L2f: Characteristic X-ray lines have energies that depend only on the beam energy of the incoming electrons and not on the element in the target.
Q119.L3f: The sharp lines come from bombarding electrons moving faster than the speed of light in the metal, which radiate coherently at a few discrete wavelengths.
Q119.L4f: Characteristic X rays are produced by electrons emitting Čerenkov radiation as they travel through the metal.
